question: A 37-year-old nulliparous woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of heavy, prolonged bleeding with menstruation, dyspareunia, and cyclical abdominal pain. Menses previously occurred at regular 28-day intervals and lasted 4 days with normal flow. Pelvic examination shows an asymmetrically enlarged, nodular uterus consistent in size with a 10-week gestation. A urine pregnancy test is negative. A photomicrograph of a section of an endometrial biopsy specimen is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
analysis: The patient's symptoms of heavy, prolonged menstrual bleeding, dyspareunia, and cyclical abdominal pain, along with the pelvic examination findings of an asymmetrically enlarged, nodular uterus, suggest a diagnosis of leiomyoma (fibroids). The negative pregnancy test rules out pregnancy-related causes. Endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma are less likely given the age and presentation, while endometriosis typically presents with more localized pain rather than an enlarged uterus. Adenomyosis could also cause similar symptoms but is less likely to present with a distinctly nodular uterus. Therefore, leiomyoma is the most likely diagnosis.
